passages.happening:
The daughters of Jerusalem ask, ‘Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women? Which way has he turned? We will seek him with you’ (verse 1).

She answers that she knows: ‘My beloved has gone down to his garden, to the beds of spices, to pasture his flock in the gardens and to gather lilies’ (verse 2). And then: ‘I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me; he pastures his flock among the lilies’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 5 ended in pain: she hesitated, he withdrew, she was beaten in the streets, and she praised him to the daughters of Jerusalem. Chapter 6 picks up at once, and her answer shows that the separation was never as final as it felt. He is in his garden, and she belongs to him.

In love poetry across the ancient world the garden was a common picture of the beloved woman and of closeness. Egyptian love songs use similar pictures of gardens, trees and fragrance.

Verse 3 nearly reverses 2:16. There she said first that he was hers. Here she begins with her belonging to him. The belonging runs both ways.
passages.later: The Bible's opening pages put man and woman in a garden together, made for each other: ‘And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, where He placed the man He had formed’ (Genesis 2:8).
passages.asks: She says she belongs to her beloved, and he to her. Ask what belonging to someone has meant in your life, and what it cost and gave. And ask how you might renew a bond that has felt strained, as this chapter renews theirs.

passages.happening:
He praises her again. ‘You are as beautiful, my darling, as Tirzah, as lovely as Jerusalem, as majestic as troops with banners’ (verse 4). ‘Turn your eyes away from me, for they have overcome me’ (verse 5). He repeats his earlier praise of her hair, her teeth and her brow (verses 5-7).

‘There are sixty queens and eighty concubines, and maidens without number’ (verse 8), but his dove, his perfect one, is unique, her mother's favorite, and the women of the court praise her (verse 9).

‘Who is this who shines like the dawn, as fair as the moon, as bright as the sun, as majestic as the stars in procession?’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Tirzah was an early royal city of the northern kingdom, before King Omri moved the capital to Samaria in the ninth century BC. Its name means something like pleasing. Setting it beside Jerusalem puts two capitals side by side, which some take as a sign of an early date and others as simple poetic choice.

Her beauty is not merely pretty. Compared to an army with banners and to the dawn, moon, sun and stars, it is overwhelming, even a little frightening. The word for majestic can carry a sense of awe.

The praise in verses 5 to 7 repeats chapter 4 almost word for word, as though the relationship has been restored and the old words of admiration can be said again.

Sixty queens and eighty concubines evoke a royal household like Solomon's. Among all of them, he says, she alone is his. The words translated perfect one come from tam, complete, one of a kind.
passages.later: The Bible records how large Solomon's household grew: ‘He had seven hundred wives of royal birth and three hundred concubines’ (1 Kings 11:3), and it says they turned his heart away. The Song sets against that a love for one alone.
passages.hard:
Is the Song of Songs about human love or about God's love, and how should it be read?

There are several main readings, each with serious defenders.

The allegorical reading, dominant in synagogue and church for many centuries, treats the book as a picture of God and Israel, in the Targum and rabbinic midrash, or of Christ and the church or the soul, in Origen, Bernard and many others. Its strength is the Bible's frequent use of marriage for God's covenant. Its weakness is that the details often became arbitrary, with every image given a spiritual meaning.

The natural reading, now the most common among scholars, treats the Song as love poetry celebrating human desire and faithful love, whether as a collection of songs or as a loose drama with two main characters, Solomon and the woman, or three, the woman, her shepherd lover, and Solomon as a rival. Its strength is that it lets the text say what it plainly says.

A third reading tries to hold both together. The Song is first about human love, and because marriage is meant to picture God's covenant love, it can also point beyond itself.

These notes take no side. Whichever reading one takes, the book's place in Scripture says that God cares about love between a man and a woman.
passages.asks: Among many, he says, she is the only one. Ask whether the person you love knows that they are unique to you. And ask what it would mean to praise them, again, in words you have used before and still mean.

passages.t: Down to the walnut grove, and come back, O Shulammite
passages.happening:
‘I went down to the walnut grove to see the blossoms of the valley, to see if the vines were budding or the pomegranates were in bloom’ (verse 11). Before the speaker knew it, desire had set them among the royal chariots (verse 12).

Then a call: “Come back, come back, O Shulammite! Come back, come back, that we may gaze upon you” (verse 13). And another voice asks why they look at her as at a dance before two camps (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Verse 12 is one of the hardest lines in the Old Testament to translate. Older versions turned part of it into a personal name, Amminadib, and modern versions differ widely.

Shulammite is the first title the woman is given. Its meaning is debated: a woman from the village of Shunem, like Abishag the Shunammite; a feminine form matching the name Solomon; or a name linked with shalom, peace.

The dance of Mahanaim is also obscure. Mahanaim, a town in Gilead, means two camps, and the phrase may refer to a known festival dance or to dancing between two rows of onlookers.

Working out who is speaking is one of the chief difficulties of the Song. Here the woman, the friends and perhaps the man all seem to speak in a few short lines.
passages.later: Mahanaim got its name from Jacob, who met God's angels there: ‘So he named that place Mahanaim’ (Genesis 32:2). And Abishag, the young woman who served King David in his old age, was from Shunem (1 Kings 1:3).
passages.asks: The friends call her to come back so they can see her. Ask who in your life you have drifted from, and who might be glad to see you come back. And ask how you look at the people you admire: with honor, or only with wanting.
